chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Ash'ari, from Ibn al-Qaddah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Rasool-Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: 'By My Honour and My Majesty! I will not take a servant from the world while I intend to be merciful to him until I fully compensate him for every mistake (sin) he has committed, either through sickness in his body, or through constriction in his sustenance, or through fear in his worldly life. So if a remainder remains upon him, I will intensify (the punishment) for him at the time of death.'

And by My Honour and My Majesty! I will not take a servant from the world while I intend to punish him until I fully fulfill for him every good deed he has done, either through expansion in his sustenance, or through health in his body, or through security in his worldly life. So if a remainder remains upon him, I will ease the death for him because of it.'
ai.seo_question: How does God compensate for sins and reward good deeds in this world before death?
ai.summary: This hadith qudsi, recorded in al-Kafi, elucidates the concept of 'Hastening of Punishment' (Tasri' al-'Iqab) by framing worldly afflictions as expiatory mechanisms for sins and worldly blessings as deferred rewards for the wicked. Scholarly tradition interprets this as a manifestation of divine mercy, where the believer's minor sins are purged through physical or financial trials, ensuring a cleaner state at death. The text highlights the dual nature of divine justice, where the balance of deeds is settled either through immediate worldly experience or at the moment of transition.
